The Final Ad Checklist Before BFCM – What To Fix Now & What To Leave via @sejournal, @tonyadam

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your Black Friday advertising should now be built, paced, and approved.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is the checklist our team works through on the accounts we run through the end of the holiday season.
  • If you have not built campaigns by now, you are really cutting it close and leaving it for last minute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your Black Friday advertising should now be built, paced, and approved. The useful work left is checking what’s running will continue running and being honest about anything that isn’t ready. Some of it can still be fixed in the few days before Black Friday on Nov. 27, and some of it belongs on next year’s plan.

Recent findings suggest that this is the checklist our team works through on the accounts we run through the end of the holiday season. Most of this is dull stuff, sure, but the last thing you want is something like this breaking at the worst possible time. So think of it like our checklist being passed on to you to make sure that doesn’t happen.

If you have not built campaigns by now, you are really cutting it close and leaving it for last minute. For the accounts we run, the freeze date was last Friday, Nov. 20, and since then the only changes going in are fixes or tweaks. Any major changes now could trigger you right back into learning mode, and you don’t want that. Campaigns should be structured, stable, and running leading into Black Friday Cyber Monday (BFCM).

If something still isn’t built, only launch low-risk pieces, like a brand campaign if you somehow don’t have one, or promo creative inside an asset group or ad set that already has history. Anything structural goes on next year’s blueprint.

Pacing should have started in early November, so budgets are already close to where you want them on Black Friday instead of sitting at an October level waiting for one massive jump on Thursday. Frankly speaking, most companies start their BFCM offers early, so if that’s you, you have nothing to worry about here because you might already be ramped up.

Industry observers note that on Meta, the ramp should have happened in steps, since frequent budget changes can send ad sets back into learning. Meta’s developer documentation describes budget scheduling as a way to “schedule budget increases for your campaign or ad set budget” for days when you expect higher sales. If you scheduled increases, check the dates and amounts against your sale.

Industry observers note that on Google, a campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day, and no more than 30.4 times the average daily budget over the month. When you change a budget partway through the month, Google recalculates the monthly limit as what you’ve spent so far plus the upcoming daily budget times the remaining calendar days, counting the day of the edit.

Cyber Monday 2026 falls on Nov. 30, the last day of the month, so if you raise a budget that morning, the monthly limit becomes what you’ve spent plus one day of the fresh budget, and you won’t be charged for more than that one day regardless of the 2x daily allowance. A campaign that runs close to double its budget Friday through Sunday is also using the monthly room Cyber Monday would have had. So treat Black Friday through Cyber Monday as one stretch, set those budgets before the weekend, and check on Sunday night how much monthly room your key campaigns have left.

Google’s campaign total budgets let you set one budget for a three- to 90-day window on Performance Max, Search, and Shopping, but they’re only available for latest campaigns, so this isn’t the week to start using them. The monthly limit starts over on Dec. 1, so set December budgets now as well.

If budgets haven’t ramped, raise Google budgets today, since the change takes effect immediately and the rest of the month paces to the fresh number. On Meta, start stepping budgets up today rather than all at once on Thursday night. And write down the budget you wish you’d had on November 1, because that’s where next year’s ramp starts.

See also: Google Ads Channel Priorities Have Limits – What PMax Still Won’t Let You Split.

A few things can’t be checked in a settings screen, so these are the questions I’d want an honest answer to before Thursday, and what I’d do if the answer is no.

Recent findings suggest that prospecting funded in September and October is what pays during BFCM. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, which is why I argued that September was the last month to fund it. Your own lag depends on price point and how long people take to decide.

If the answer is no: Don’t launch cold prospecting this week, when in our accounts prospecting CPMs are at their highest of the year. Keep the prospecting you have on a flat budget through the week and let harvest campaigns take the extra money. Put the build on next year’s calendar for September, as a fixed budget rather than a percentage of whatever is left.

Sources indicate that it should lean towards Bottom Of Funnel (BoFu). BFCM is when the demand you built in the fall turns into orders, so retargeting, brand search, and your existing customers are going to take a bigger share of spend than they do the rest of the year. During the holidays, those sales are worth buying. What matters is that it was a decision. Before the week starts, you should know roughly how much budget is going to people who already know you, how much stays on latest customers, and what the floor is for prospecting so it doesn’t get raided the first time retargeting looks great on Friday morning.

Keep in mind that during BFCM, your email, SMS, retargeting, and brand campaigns are often all reaching the same person for the same order, and each one will report it. So don’t move budget into retargeting just because its ROAS looks great on Black Friday. Check it against what the store is actually doing overall before you add more.

You can see the split on both platforms. On Google, lifecycle goal reporting adds a “Newly introduced vs. returning customers” segment to the Campaigns table on campaigns where the new customer acquisition goal is turned on, and on Meta, audience segments break sales campaign results into new, engaged, and existing customers once you’ve defined them in your ad account settings.

If the answer is no: Decide it today. Write down the prospecting floor and the rough share for fresh versus existing customers through Cyber Monday, and look at the new versus returning numbers each morning so you’re adjusting against the blueprint instead of against whichever campaign has the best ROAS that day.

You should by now. Testing is what October is for, and BFCM is when you have winning creative you know you can put advertising dollars against. That matters most on Meta, where the creative is doing most of the targeting in Advantage+, so in our accounts, a proven concept with the offer added to it tends to beat a brand newly introduced idea during holiday shopping. The offer can go on as an overlay, in the first few seconds of a video, or in the headline, without changing what made the ad work in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that if the answer is no: Look back at the last 60 to 90 days, pick the best performer on each platform by cost per purchase, and add the offer to that. Don’t run a creative test during the most expensive week of the year, because whatever wins under BFCM pricing won’t tell you much about January. Put an October testing window on next year’s initiative, so you go into the holiday season with your winners already picked.

Sources indicate that every date through December should have creative approved and paused: Black Friday, Cyber Monday, any Cyber Week extension, shipping deadlines, last-minute gifts and gift cards, and post-Christmas on Dec. 26.

Google’s ad review page says most ads are reviewed within one business day and “changes to your ad or assets restart the review process and may cause delays.” Meta’s Marketing API best practices say changes to creative or targeting trigger review and that an ad entering review while paused stays paused after approval.

If the answer is no: Submit what’s missing today with final copy and schedule it with end dates, because Thanksgiving week is short on business days and a typo caught after approval means another trip through review.

Place a real order with your promo code and follow it into Google Ads and Meta Events Manager. A tag check only confirms that something fired, and a checkout change made in November can alter the value your purchase event sends without stopping it from firing.

If something is off, it’s worth pulling a developer in before Wednesday. If tracking breaks during the week anyway, fix it and apply a data exclusion so the bidder doesn’t learn from the broken days. Cancel the test order afterward.

The site banner, landing page, sale price in your feed, Merchant Center promotions, and ad copy should all say the same thing, because a mismatch usually reveals up as disapprovals the morning the sale starts. Merchant Center’s automatic item updates are on by default and correct prices from your landing pages, but Google says they may not work for products whose price changes more than once a day.

Push your own feed updates for any hourly doorbusters, run a purchase on the promo landing page from a phone the way a customer would, and name the person who opens Merchant Center diagnostics first thing Black Friday.

Industry observers note that billing is the item most likely to stop every ad you have. Google says a declined payment can stop the account, and on monthly invoicing, once costs reach the account budget, “all ads in the account stop running.” On Meta, the ad account spend cap is a hard stop, and “when the amount is reached, all delivery stops.”.

Raise the invoiced account budget to cover the higher spend through Nov. 30, reset any Meta spend cap, check the card on file, and give at least two people admin access on both platforms and Merchant Center, with two-step verification on devices they’ll have over the holiday.

Several Google Ads features that add promotions or pick landing pages are on by default, so go through them before your own promotion goes live.

According to recent reports, I wouldn’t switch all of this off on principle. Decide on each one during the holidays and note what you changed so you can revisit it in January.

Your brand campaign should be fully funded through Cyber Monday, and even into December. Keep an eye on auction insights daily to see which competitors are bidding on your brand. I know I’m stating the obvious, but this is definitely not the time of the year to let a competitor steal a brand sale. Be defensive, buy your brand terms, and keep that impression share % high. Keeping brand in its own campaign, which I’ve argued for before, makes a “Limited By Budget” status obvious the morning it happens.

On one premium brand we work with, several competitors were bidding on the brand name, and we’ve consistently managed brand spend throughout the year, but during holiday shopping times, we max out impression share %.

Once the checks are done, the hardest part of Black Friday advertising is leaving the account alone and letting it run. Of course, make sure there is someone keeping an eye on it from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday and have a plan in place for what can change. Does pacing increase at all? If so, what % increase is the cap? Should any creative be swapped out? Messaging?

Sources indicate that we keep that checklist pretty short: budgets on campaigns that are hitting target and fixes for tracking or disapprovals, and everything else waits until Dec. 1.

According to recent reports, keep a running list throughout the week of anything you couldn’t fix, whether that’s prospecting you never built, creative you didn’t get to test, or the budget you wish you’d started with in early November. It’s the most useful thing you’ll have when you start planning next year’s holiday season, and it’s a lot easier to write down this week than to piece together in January, or even next year.

Featured Image: Master1305/Shutterstock.

According to recent reports, check that budgets have ramped, that tracking records the right value on a real promo order, that billing won’t stop your ads, and that your offer matches across site, feed, and ads. Campaigns and creative should already be built, so the week is for checks and fixes.

Industry observers note that enough that your best campaigns aren’t capped on Black Friday or Cyber Monday, based on your own past results rather than a round number. With Cyber Monday on November 30, set Google budgets before the weekend, since a budget raised on the last day of the month only gets one day of room.

Industry observers note that for this year, mostly yes. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, so prospecting rolled out now is bought at peak prices and mostly pays out in January. Keep what you have running and initiative next year’s build for September.

Sources indicate that no. Results from BFCM week don’t carry over well to the rest of the year, and an untested concept is an expensive bet at peak prices. Put the offer on proven creative and test in October.

Yes. If competitors bid on your brand and you don’t, you can lose those sales to them. Keep brand in its own campaign with enough budget and check auction insights daily through Cyber Week.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
  • Our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end users, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk.
  • think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

Our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end users, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk. We are hiring a Security Engineer to build and run our vulnerability management and security operations program. Vulnerability management is a core capability for keeping our security posture strong as the platform and the manufacturer grow: knowing what we run, finding what is exposed, and getting the right fixes shipped quickly. It also underpins our customer commitments and the compliance programs we are building. Our program is early, and you will shape it. You will join a small Trust team that covers security, IT and compliance, and you will own this program end to end from your first week.

think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.

take an automation-first and pragmatic approach to risk mitigation.

translate security concerns into engineering action.

can clearly explain complex technical concepts to others.

are a fast learner and thrive in ambiguity.

Select, deploy and operationalize scanning tooling across our production assets.

Run vulnerability management end to end: triage, severity in our environment, owner assignment, remediation SLAs and reporting.

Build engineering-first triage and remediation workflows that fit how our engineering teams already work, and automate the routing and follow-up.

Build a remediation dashboard that engineering and leadership read and act on.

Automate collection of the vulnerability management evidence our compliance programs depend on, in partnership with our Compliance team.

Build automation, including agentic tooling, that removes manual security operations work and keeps pace with engineering growth.

5+ years in security engineering, security operations or software engineering, with a significant share of that focused on security.

Hands-on experience building or running a vulnerability management program or software security tooling (SCA, container, cloud or host scanning).

An engineering-first approach to triage and remediation: you get findings fixed by making the fix easy to ship.

The judgment to set a finding's real severity in our environment, using CVSS as one input.

Strong scripting and automation skills in a language such as Go or Python, and comfort reading infrastructure as code such as Terraform.

A pragmatic approach to risk: you can explain why a finding matters to the business and how fast it needs to be fixed.

Experience with real-time media, networking or WebRTC systems.

Experience supporting compliance audits such as HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

Incident response or application security experience.

Experience in AI security, such as securing LLM applications or agent infrastructure.

An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

Competitive salary and equity package.

Health, dental, and vision benefits.

According to recent reports, liveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.

From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

It’s been yet another busy week. Recap it with the fourth edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

Recent findings suggest that the Chicago Sun-Times announced a new slogan this week. What is it?

“Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this company voted this week to authorize a strike.

“The union has been negotiating a fresh contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”.

Industry observers note that A “digital experience platform” company whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

A major journalism school announced this week that its master’s degree programs would now be tuition-free for in-state residents. Which school?

“Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for New Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”.

At this week’s summit in China, Bloomberg TV reporter Annmarie Hordern asked Donald Trump whether he felt Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. What happened next?

“It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.”.

Paid digital subscriptions at McClatchy-owned publications — a group that includes the Miami Herald, the Kansas City Star, and the Charlotte Observer — have declined how much in the past year, according to an internal corporate presentation?

In a recent development, unique visitors have also dropped by 39%. McClatchy’s response? Doubling down on AI.

This is the per capita annual funding for public media across a set of five rich countries: $110, $81, $53, $27, $3. Name the five countries, in order.

With prospects for public media brighter with a Democratic Congress, some advocates are calling for a major increase in the United States’ historically puny funding levels.

It has been revealed that youTube has found a latest way to inflate the number of “views” a video on its platform gets. What is it?

“YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also notes the change will help it align with ‘TV industry standards,’ which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows.”.

Sources indicate that in Czechia, mass rallies in support of public broadcasting have featured protestors wearing a very specific hat. Whose hat is it?

Since 1965, Večerníček (a diminutive of večerník, meaning evening newspaper) has appeared on Czech Television every night at 6:45 p.m. to wish children goodnight. Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government intends to scrap public media license fees.

The most important stories about journalism and the future of news, delivered to your inbox every afternoon.

Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today's media ecosystem.

Stations in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

ProPublica notes November has been the busiest month ever for its tips line.

Is “seen on the Orange Line” the new “overheard on the Acela”?

It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEProPublica wanted to find more sources in the federal government. So it brought a truck.Neel DhaneshaMarch 31, 2025ProPublica reported on potential intends to overhaul the Smithsonian on Monday. Alec MacGillis and Andy Kroll wrote that the plans, if enacted, “would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.”.

But how did MacGillis and Kroll get their hands on the explosive 25-item list? An open laptop, a crowded D.C. Metro train, and a quick-thinking tipster. From the ProPublica piece:.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

The ProPublica reporters, going off initials seen on the laptop, searched White House staffing records and “took to the Orange Line,” hoping it was a regular route for the staffer.

In a recent development, sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint.

Kroll told me that he and MacGillis made three trips to different parts of the Orange Line to report out the tip.

“That included me standing outside for a few hours in a Metro station on an especially cold morning with a woefully insufficient coat on,” Kroll added. “Not the most glamorous reporting assignment, but important to getting the story.”.

Industry observers note that we’ve covered ProPublica’s creative attempts to reach prospective tipsters — which include an LED billboard truck and public transit ads in the Washington, D.C. area — in the past. The nonprofit investigative outlet has been a news industry leader in crowdsourcing and engagement reporting.

ProPublica engagement and tips coordinator Adriana Pera told me that the tips line has been “very, very busy.” In November, ProPublica received its “highest number of tips to date,” Pera said. At least 20 ProPublica investigations in the last year started with sensitive information delivered through the tips line.

According to recent reports, during a recent conference for the Association of the United States Army (AUSA), the largest annual gathering of Army contractors, Pera and others handed out flyers. ProPublica also purchased ads on bus shelters they thought attendees were likely to walk by.

“We’re always looking for ways to reach the people we need to reach, in the places they’re likeliest to be, based on our reporting needs,” Mel Kramer, engagement team product manager, said. “A good tips line is both staffed and comes to mind swiftly. When someone sees something that investigative reporters should see, we want them to think of ProPublica.”.

Sources indicate that up next for the team? Handing out coasters in sports bars to collect info on sports betting.

Google Notes Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Searchenginejournal

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.
  • Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ says, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.
  • Google’s Search Central changelog notes the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.

Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ says, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.

Google’s Search Central changelog notes the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy. I covered the policy when Google declared it in April, with enforcement set to start June 15.

One FAQ question asks whether the back button hijacking policy covers people who arrive from a non-Search channel, such as social media, and then can’t get back to where they came from. Google wrote:.

“If back button hijacking happens when a user is browsing within a browser, then the policy applies.”.

A separate answer states “Discover is a part of Google Search and our spam policies apply to Discover as well.” That answer covers Google’s spam policies in general, not only this one.

For a website that opens an external app, which then keeps the user from getting back to the site, the FAQ states “app navigation and ‘open in app’ behaviors are outside the scope of the back button hijacking policy.”.

Google’s FAQ indicates how the policy applies to visits in a browser and where external app navigation falls outside its scope.

Google’s April announcement said some back button hijacking “may originate from the site’s included libraries or advertising platform,” and asked sites to remove or turn off the code behind it.

In a recent development, the FAQ asks whether Google is preventing sites from importing code hosted by advertising platforms. Google wrote:.

“No, site owners can continue to work with advertising platforms and import code that they host. We only take action on pages that exhibit back button hijacking behavior.”.

According to recent reports, A back button test that starts from a Google results page doesn’t cover every visit the hijacking policy applies to. Test pages that carry ad code by arriving from a social media link and pressing back, and repeat it from Discover when one of your pages reveals up there.

Sources indicate that google’s answer on ad code lets you keep your ad partners. The thing to remove is the code or setting on a page that interferes with the back button, wherever it comes from.

Google’s FAQ also says owners can report back button hijacking through its spam report form. Those reports go toward improving Google’s spam detection systems, which gives people who hit hijacking on a social or Discover visit a way to flag a site.

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that big gainers included W42ST, the Point/Plover Metro Wire, Grice Connect (“In the rural south, death is a large social driver”), and the Philomath News. Here’s our quarterly ranking of the top 25 local for-profit news sites in the United States.

    According to recent reports, it’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb.

    Today’s edition looks at local for-profit news sites. (Eligible sites for this ranking are for-profit members of the trade group LION Publishers — LION standing for Local, Independent, Online News — so these are mostly digital-born newsrooms, not newspapers or TV stations.) The rankings for Q3 feature many of the same sites that performed well in our last edition. This time around, we’ve got details from local news sites in New York, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nevada, Georgia, and Oregon. Below that are the Top 25 rankings for July, August, and September.

    According to recent reports, W42ST In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July. Publisher Phil O’Brien remarked that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST. “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.” O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s at the moment trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve rolled out earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week. It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said. Point/Plover Metro Wire Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski. The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said. Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said. “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.” Grice Connect Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July. DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position. But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site. Philomath News The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath. Similarweb stats showed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second major source of traffic when search dips,” he said. In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said. Oklahoma City Free Press, LINK nky, This Is Reno In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.” The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews. Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.     In Fresh York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July.

    Industry observers note that publisher Phil O’Brien mentioned that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST.

    “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.”.

    According to recent reports, O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s presently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve debuted earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week.

    In a recent development, it’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he noted.

    Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” mentioned publisher Brandi Makuski.

    Recent findings suggest that the site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski mentioned high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said.

    Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining latest customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said.

    Sources indicate that “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she mentioned. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.”.

    According to recent reports, statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July.

    DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position.

    According to recent reports, but Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect debuted free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site.

    The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath.

    Similarweb stats revealed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said.

    According to recent reports, in a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he noted.

    Sources indicate that in Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.”.

    Sources indicate that the Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews.

    In a recent development, nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.
    • Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s newly introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.
    • Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.

    Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s newly introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. After using it for a while, though, I had a nagging feeling: Is Hydrogen actually producing better answers than Gemini 3.8 Flash, or am I just assuming newer means better?

    Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.

    You can actually try the exact same six-question blind test yourself here (columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every question, and there is a button at the top to reveal how I voted and the real token costs).

    It has been revealed that the blind 3-way taste test interface: columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every SEO question, complete with clickable OKF concept pills. Try voting blind yourself here. Image Credit: Marie Haynes.

    Before I even finished reading the first round of blind outputs, one thing jumped out immediately: The answers were way too long.

    My Brain had been defaulting to Detailed mode with no word ceiling. When we checked the API logs, we discovered something wild: Gemini 4 Hydrogen was going into an over-eager research loop, reading an average of 21 OKF files per question, taking 68 seconds, writing 1,600-word essays, and costing $0.44 per prompt – actually more expensive per turn than Gemini 4 Neon!

    On top of that, some answers were dropping internal Google engineering jargon (like MAGIT and FastSearch) that a busy business owner does not need to wade through just to figure out why their clicks dropped.

    So before doing my real blind vote, I made three quick upgrades to how Marie’s Brain works:.

    Then we re-ran the exact same six real-world SEO and AI Search questions – covering AI Overviews and traffic drops, whether to delete or rewrite informational posts, Main Content on commercial buyer’s guides, pruning thin location pages, agent readiness and /llms.txt, and a realistic five-hour-a-week initiative that skips GEO distractions – across Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and Gemini 4 Neon.

    With the model names hidden and the columns randomized, I read all 18 answers and picked a winner on every prompt.

    When I hit reveal, the result wasn’t even close:.

    What stood out to me about Neon wasn’t that it had more facts – all three models pulled from the exact same OKF files. It was how it communicated. Neon’s answers felt more like a smart human thinking through a problem rather than a predictable AI response. I genuinely enjoyed reading them, and I immediately understood what they were trying to get across.

    My revealed blind test results (5/6 for Gemini 4 Neon), real Gemini API token usage, and pace-adjusted monthly cost estimates per user. Image Credit: Marie Haynes.

    Of course, better answers only matter if the economics make sense. Here are the real numbers from our live Concise-mode runs (using real Gemini API usageMetadata, including thinking tokens, at conservative uncached list rates):.

    Note on Neon’s speed: That 70.8s average was skewed by one single 3.5-minute API queue spike during testing; typical Neon replies ran 18 to 40 seconds (with text streaming on screen as it writes).

    At first glance, $191 vs. $93 per 1,000 prompts sounds like a substantial jump (about 10 cents extra per prompt). But when I mapped that against realistic full-month usage paces extrapolated from my early active customers, here is what the extra cost per user looks like:.

    And those are conservative uncached estimates. Because every turn references the same ~55,000-token OKF Master Index, Gemini 4 Neon’s implicit context caching discounts repeated input tokens across multi-turn chats, bringing real-world bills noticeably lower.

    Check Who’s Posting Before You Trust Reddit On AEO Tools via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Graphite flagged 55% of the users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.
    • Among the users it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.
    • The growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Graphite flagged 55% of the users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.

    Among the users it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.

    The growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool. OpenAI language models labeled the mentions, the opinions and the likely promoters.

    The agency helps companies with AEO and SEO and states it doesn’t sell AEO tools or accept payment to be mentioned. Its CEO, Ethan Smith, is an investor in Peec AI, one of three tools tied for the highest score in the analysis.

    Graphite flagged 1,298 of the 2,365 Reddit owners who gave an opinion of an AEO tool or a marketing platform’s AEO features.

    It has been revealed that A user was flagged when the agency’s model put the chance at 50% or more that their posts promoted a marketing product they build, own, work for, sell or partner with. That includes SEO, AEO, sales and web analytics tools. An agency’s description of its own client work did not constitute promotion.

    In a recent development, to test the model, the firm manually inspected 43 of the people it had flagged. Ultimately, 12% of them disclosed being promoters, while 62% were found to have promoted a product but failed to identify themselves as such; the remaining ones were judged non-promoters. The write-up also indicates that some of the models’ labeling decisions could be incorrect.

    Sources indicate that four types of likely promoter Reddit accounts were identified. Each type exhibited a pattern across several posts or comments.

    One account was used to recommend the same lesser-known tracking service on eight posts and comments. In January this user claimed that they switched from a competitor, and 11 days later they commented about possibly purchasing the product.

    Another account made reference to a little-known product in four comments with well-known tracking services over the course of eight days.

    A third account posted three separate times for the same product within 12 minutes.

    It has been revealed that over six weeks, 38 accounts recommended the same product in 52 comments, each using the phrase “from what I’ve read” in its recommendation. That phrase appears with any other tool no more than twice.

    Of the opinions regarding the accuracy of AEO tools from users who weren’t flagged, 143 were negative while 27 had positive views. No other feature elicited as many negative opinions. These users provided opinions on 44 tools, for a total of 1,557 opinions.

    Graphite’s chart compares praise and criticism across features after excluding opinions from consumers it flagged as likely promoters.

    Industry observers note that according to the write-up, users frequently view visibility scores as estimates due to variation in AI answers among different runs, locations and users. Several have advised fellow users to “treat them as trend, not truth” and to verify the information through manual review.

    According to recent reports, the citation data, or the citations used by AI systems as source material for their answers, was generally viewed positively by consumers. Price received more user opinions than any other attribute and most of those opinions were negative, at 182 negative versus 98 positive.

    Industry observers note that the agency also evaluated the 11 tools which generated sufficient opinions using a 0-100 point scale; a score of 50 represented neutral. Each of the 11 tools scored between 54 and 66 points. The authors also said the ranges around many of the tools’ scores overlapped and therefore, the differences in scores could lack statistical significance.

    Graphite’s count puts a number on how many Reddit users weighing in on AEO tools may be promoting marketing software. Before a tool recommended on Reddit goes on your shortlist, check the account’s history for repeat plugs and a story that changes from post to post.

    Graphite’s tool scores reflect opinions from January through September, and the manufacturer says their order could change as more opinions come in. Complaints about the accuracy of visibility scores give you something to test before renewing. Run a sample of your tracked prompts by hand and compare the results with the tool’s numbers.

    Featured Image: Accogliente Design/Shutterstock.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Director of Technology Partnerships to lead the teams responsible for growing Supabase through technology integrations and our marketplace ecosystem.

    You’ll bring together two complementary motions: partnerships that embed Supabase into the products developers already use, and a marketplace that helps developers discover and connect complementary technologies to their Supabase projects. Your job is to turn both into durable sources of revenue, adoption, and customer value.

    Industry observers note that reporting to the Head of Partnerships, you’ll lead and develop the Integrations and Marketplace teams, set their commercial strategy, and work hands-on with our most notable partners. A central part of the role is working closely with AI labs to build strategic relationships, develop integrations, and bring joint opportunities to market. You’ll partner closely with Product, Engineering, Sales, Marketing, and Finance to take integrations from idea to launch—and grow their impact long after launch.

    Recent findings suggest that this role is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, where you’ll build relationships with leading AI, developer tools, and infrastructure companies. Supabase is remote-first, and you’ll work across a globally distributed team.

    Lead, coach, and develop the Integrations and Marketplace partnerships teams, including team leads and partner managers.

    Set a clear strategy for where Supabase invests across strategic technology partnerships, marketplace categories, and emerging ecosystem opportunities.

    Define team objectives, partner coverage, investment priorities, and operating cadence. Make thoughtful tradeoffs between high-touch strategic partnerships and scalable programs.

    Build a culture of ownership, commercial discipline, and strong cross-functional execution.

    Drive revenue from technology integrations through partner-driven customer acquisition, product consumption, expansion, retention, co-sell opportunities, and commercial arrangements.

    Own the commercial performance of the technology partnerships and marketplace portfolio, including forecasting and reporting on progress, risks, and return on investment.

    Build and deepen relationships with AI labs, working closely with their product, engineering, business development, and executive teams to identify and execute high-impact partnership opportunities.

    Develop executive relationships with strategic partners across developer tools, cloud, and adjacent infrastructure.

    Lead or support negotiations for complex partnerships, including integration, referral, revenue-sharing, and joint go-to-market agreements.

    Help partner managers build joint business plans that connect partner priorities to measurable outcomes for Supabase and its customers.

    Lead and develop the Marketplace team, setting its commercial and partner strategy and holding the team accountable for outcomes.

    Guide the team in identifying the capabilities developers need, recruiting the right partners, and helping those partners launch and grow.

    Set priorities and allocate resources across strategic, high-touch partners and scalable paths for emerging and self-serve partners.

    Ensure the team works effectively with Product and Engineering on integration quality, partner onboarding, discovery, activation, and the developer experience across product surfaces.

    Enable the team to work with Marketing and Sales to launch integrations, enable teams, and drive ongoing adoption—not just announcements.

    Establish clear measures for partner-sourced and influenced pipeline, integration adoption, revenue, consumption, retention, and marketplace performance.

    Work with Finance, Data, and Partner Operations to improve attribution, reporting, forecasting, and partner revenue processes.

    Represent the voice of partners and customers in product and go-to-market planning, while aligning stakeholders around shared priorities.

    Identify risks early, remove blockers, and communicate decisions and outcomes clearly to leadership.

    Have significant experience in technology partnerships, business development, or ecosystem leadership at a developer tools, cloud, infrastructure, or SaaS manufacturer.

    Have led and developed partner-facing teams, including managers or senior individual contributors, and can balance strategic direction with hands-on execution.

    Have a track record of building partnerships that produced measurable revenue, product adoption, or customer growth.

    Have negotiated complex commercial agreements and understand partnership economics, including revenue share, referrals, and consumption-based models.

    Have worked closely with Product and Engineering to ship and grow technical integrations. You can engage credibly with technical teams, including those at AI labs, even if you aren’t the person writing the code.

    Know how to build relationships with executives while earning the trust of product, engineering, and go-to-market teams.

    Use data to prioritize opportunities, assess partner performance, and make decisions when attribution is imperfect.

    Are comfortable building in an evolving environment, communicating in writing, and working asynchronously across time zones.

    Built or scaled a developer marketplace, integration ecosystem, or partner platform.

    Worked with AI LLMs, AI app builders, databases, open-source products, or developer infrastructure.

    A background in software development, with an understanding of how developers build and integrate products.

    Experience growing both a small number of strategic partnerships and a broader, scalable partner program.

    A strong network in the San Francisco Bay Area technology ecosystem.

    In a recent development, we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Sources indicate that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    According to recent reports, once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    In a recent development, supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Recent findings suggest that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #158420. Breaking: Mail Metro Media’s next creator play is representing them

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1300 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Mail Metro Media’s next creator play is representing them

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • Mail Metro Media now thinks “more like a talent agency” and commissions “like a broadcaster”, according to Hannah Blake, its managing director of creator and new media.
    • Industry observers note that audiences tune in for them, brands pay to reach those audiences, and the deals have grown from around £5,000 apiece to worth seven figures in October.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Mail Metro Media now thinks “more like a talent agency” and commissions “like a broadcaster”, according to Hannah Blake, its managing director of creator and new media. Its creators have, in other words, become the business.

    Industry observers note that audiences tune in for them, brands pay to reach those audiences, and the deals have grown from around £5,000 apiece to worth seven figures in October. Holding on to those creators is now as important as finding them since any one who leaves for an outside agent can take the audience and advertisers along too.

    Blake spelled out that risk on stage at the Digiday Media Strategies London event in October.

    “The huge risk is that we make these people super famous and then they go and get signed by a different agent,” she stated.

    So in September the ad sales arm for the Daily Mail hired David White from Whalar as head of creators, with a brief to build an in-house talent agency that represents its creators and signs outside talent too. White was the first hire for the company’s Stars business in Newly introduced York, the talent management arm that handles creators’ careers beyond brand deals and was also a senior talent manager there.

    What the business ultimately ends up with is still open. Blake described something that “potentially could look more like a talent agency and an employer,” and she hopes to have it in market by the end of the year. The final shape matters because running a talent agency would be a big change of job for a newspaper group’s ad sales team. It exists to sell audiences to brands while an agent’s job is to get the best deal for the talent. Mail Metro Media would be trying to do both at once.

    According to recent reports, that’s the potted history of how Mail Metro Media reached this point. The full story is a lot more nuanced.

    Industry observers note that it started four years ago when Daily Mail launched Eliza, a social-only brand for young women fronted by six fashion and beauty creators. Its hit format, “Guess Which Outfit’s Most Expensive”, puts two women on the street, one in a £10,000 outfit and the other in a high-street copy, and leaves viewers to guess which is which. It kept going viral, people kept coming back and advertisers soon followed. That’s despite it being relatively small next to the rest of the Mail’s portfolio, and yet “we were doing lots of direct advertisers relationships quite quickly”, Blake remarked. Fast forward to now,  and brands often book content on Eliza and then want its creators posting on their own accounts too, which Mail Metro Media packages into the deal.

    The Mail’s own TikTok was a different story. The Mail and Metro launched on the platform around the same time as Eliza and the former became the biggest news publisher there, with 20 million followers, on the back of rapid-fire news clips. But the money didn’t follow. “The huge issue was there was no monetization there,” Blake remarked, even though publishers had widely expected TikTok to start paying them for views. Advertisers weren’t keen either, Every rival was posting the same kind of clips and the Daily Mail couldn’t build a brand into footage it had brought in from elsewhere.

    Together, they showed the publisher that the money was in highlights it owned and creators audiences came back for. It shifted course accordingly, and over the past year it relaunched the Mail and Metro on social around repeatable shows it owns, such as the sports debate show “Dugout Debate” with creators at the front and helping shape them. Blake noted the operation now pulls 5 billion monthly video views across 10 brands and signed its first seven-figure deal last month. With that success comes a new kind of risk. The creators fronting those shows have built followings of their own and “now some of the superstars are beginning to emerge,” Blake said. Left unchecked, the publisher ends up making stars for outside agencies to sign.

    Industry observers note that in some ways, the publisher has already been acting like an agent of sorts. Alongside its core bundle where brands pay one flat rate for a run of content with “no differentiation between the talent,” Blake said it has spent the past year selling individual creators on their own channels. It calls this add-on “Creator Amp.” One example is Mimi Yates, a young journalist who fronts much of the news output and has built a following of her own. Brands can book her as part of a wider campaign or on her own, and on their personal accounts the creators “all set their own rates,” Blake said.

    That arrangement was easy to manage while the talent was still unknown.

    Industry observers note that “When we started, our creators were all emerging,” Blake stated. With bigger names now coming through, the publisher wants something sturdier. “We are now at the point where we’re beginning to formalize that relationship a bit more,” she said, and hiring White was the first step.

    He will recruit from two places. One is from its own staff. The other is outside talent Blake described as “the next generation of emerging news and entertainment talent”.

    Moves like this bring some awkward conversations with them. Daily Mail’s creators are salaried and Nathan Aspell, director of the New Media division, remarked the company owns the IP they develop. Blake described those same creators setting their own rates on their own channels. How the money is split between the employer and agent will go a long way to deciding whether a breakout star sticks around.

    Axel Springer’s version hands journalists a share of the financial results in return for production, marketing and distribution. Daily Mail hasn’t remarked what its agency will charge.

    Then there’s the small matter of journalism. The same person can read the headlines and sell the mascara, and the publisher would be both their employer and their agent. That’s a lot of hats for one newsroom.

    Recent findings suggest that white’s first signings will show how far the publisher aims to take this venture. Blake thinks publishers are headed this way regardless. “I actually think it’s just a byproduct of where the opportunity is,” she remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that for a lot of publishers, signing talent still feels like someone else’s business and talk of newsrooms turning into agencies tends to raise eyebrows. Blake sees it as following the money, which increasingly sits with “people-centric IP that exists across multiple different touchpoints”.

    Plenty of rivals are following it too. Axel Springer introduced its own spin on the same idea last month, while Hearst did so earlier this week. Increasingly, publishers see a talent operation as the next step in their latest pivot to video, which runs on personalities whose audiences, and the ad money chasing them, follow them wherever they go.

    “Publishers are responding to the audience’s desire for personality-led formats while limiting strategic dependence on individual journalists and managing talent,” noted Laura Darcey, research analyst at Enders Analysis.

    It has been revealed that editor’s note: An earlier version of this article noted David White ran Whalar’s Stars business in Upcoming York. He was the first hire for the division in New York.

    Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

    Consulting giants Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

    Breaking: Senior Contracts Manager at Supabase

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • We are looking for a Senior Contracts Manager to take ownership of vendor contracting at Supabase.
    • This is a hands-on, high-autonomy role with real ownership, for an experienced negotiator who takes pride in making procurement faster while managing risk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We are looking for a Senior Contracts Manager to take ownership of vendor contracting at Supabase. You will be the go-to contracts partner for everything we buy.

    This is a hands-on, high-autonomy role with real ownership, for an experienced negotiator who takes pride in making procurement faster while managing risk. You will negotiate directly, build the playbooks and workflows that let the business self-serve on low-risk deals, and escalate the right challenges to Legal at the right time. We work AI-first in Legal: you will use Claude and Ironclad every day to move faster and with greater accuracy. Your work will shape how procurement and vendor contracting scale as Supabase grows.

    Own vendor contracting end to end.

    Review, draft, and negotiate a high volume of vendor agreements, including MSAs, order forms, SOWs, SaaS and cloud subscription terms, DPAs, and NDAs.

    Serve as the single point of contact for all vendor contracting matters raised by FinOps, IT, Security, and business owners, from intake through signature, renewals, amendments, disputes, and offboarding. As capacity allows, you will also support the broader Commercial Legal team on other matters.

    Apply and further build out our playbook and risk framework independently, and escalate to the Assistant General Counsel, Commercial where a deal falls outside approved positions or raises novel legal risk.

    Negotiate data, privacy, and security terms (DPAs, security exhibits, cross-border transfers) within the Security team’s playbook, and bring in the AGC, Commercial or Privacy for anything outside it.

    Review AI vendor terms, such as training on our data, output ownership, and model changes.

    Build and scale vendor contracting operations.

    Build out and maintain our vendor playbook in Claude, so the whole team works from the same guidance and low-risk deals move without bottlenecks.

    Design and improve intake, triage, and approval workflows with FinOps.

    In a recent development, own the vendor and procurement workflow in Ironclad, including intake, templates, approvals, and the repository, working with Legal Ops, who own the platform. Use it to track renewals and notice windows with FinOps and flag spend concentration risks.

    Create training and self-serve resources for business partners, and raise the visibility of the contracts function as a business enabler.

    Recent findings suggest that 6 to 8+ years of experience negotiating procurement, vendor, or technology transactions contracting, ideally buy-side at a U.S. SaaS or technology manufacturer, with deep knowledge of SaaS, cloud, and software licensing terms.

    A track record of negotiating directly with vendors and their counsel, independently and at pace.

    Strong working knowledge of privacy, data protection, and security terms in commercial contracts, including DPA negotiation and international data transfers.

    Experience designing contracting processes that are consistent, transparent, and easy for the business to follow.

    Clear writing and speaking, with the ability to explain legal and commercial risk plainly and the judgment to know when to hold a position, approve a reasonable risk, or escalate.

    Comfort using AI tools, Claude in particular, with sound judgment about when to rely on outputs, how to verify them, and how to protect confidential information.

    A degree in a relevant field (for example, law, economics, or political science), though we value experience over the specific degree.

    Sell-side experience negotiating customer, partner, or reseller agreements for a SaaS or technology company, which helps you see vendor terms from the other side.

    Hands-on experience with Ironclad or a similar CLM tool (Juro, Docusign CLM) or building AI-assisted legal workflows, ideally with some exposure to AI governance.

    Experience working across jurisdictions or with distributed, international teams.

    Experience at a fast-growing, developer-focused, cloud, security, or open source company.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are notable to us.

    Once a year, the entire company gathers in a newly introduced city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    According to recent reports, supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Recent findings suggest that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.
