    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • This Media Buying Briefing covers the latest in agency news and media buying for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Monday at 10 a.m.
    • So many surprises came out of the midterm elections, and only one of them was the rout by Democrats over Republicans on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This Media Buying Briefing covers the latest in agency news and media buying for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Monday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    So many surprises came out of the midterm elections, and only one of them was the rout by Democrats over Republicans on Nov. 3 and in the days following.

    There’s a lot to be unpacked as to what impact the $12.06 billion spent during the 2025-2026 election cycle had, according to AdImpact’s revised numbers post-election, but let’s start with the fact that the outlay was the most of any cycle on record and $460 million (4%) more than AdImpact’s last projection in June.

    It’s also the first time a midterm election outspent a presidential election — which only portends even more to be spent in 2028’s presidential race.

    Why did Republicans fare so poorly when they outspent Democrat candidates overall? According to AdImpact, Republican candidates dropped $5.51 billion, a 27% hike over the 2024 cycle, compared to Dems’ $5.11 billion, which actually represented a 4% drop.

    Industry observers note that in light of that, it’s fair to ask whether political advertising still delivers the same impact and effect on voters as it had in a simpler media environment. More specifically, is TV still the way to influence voters? The answer leans toward no, since TV still attracted the most dollars, with both broadcast and streaming growing their ad dollars.

    Industry observers note that “Reaching voters and engaging them are two different things. Ads build awareness. On their own, they don’t persuade anyone or get them to the polls,” said Travis Trawick, CEO of FullPAC, a nonpartisan political technology firm. “The shift is from talking at voters to talking with them. The technology exists today to have two-way conversations at scale, see what’s landing and feed it straight back into strategy while there’s still time to act on it.”.

    Sources indicate that the numbers generally support that tech-forward approach. Looking again at post-election AdImpact data, broadcast TV set a record $5.85 billion, up 9% from 2024, as its share of spend edged up from 48% to 49%. CTV rose 14% to $2.66 billion, while digital media rose 11% to $1.91 billion. Media losing share included cable (−7%), radio (−13%), and satellite (−7%).

    Recent findings suggest that but what about the hottest thing in media buying right now, creators? Political candidates turned to them heavily in this cycle. New research from creator marketing firm Kyra, which works with SharkNinja, H&M and L’Oréal to run influencer campaigns across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, showed a strong swing in influence for Democratic-leaning creators. D-leaning creator posts drew 329.9 million views from 923 posts by 146 creators, while Republican-leaning ones drew 37 million from 170 posts by 27 creators — about 9 to 1 in views and 5 to 1 in posts.

    (One crucial caveat that Kyra noted in its research: its YouTube data is “thin [with 9.9 million views], and we don’t cover X, podcasts, Rumble or long-form YouTube, where right-leaning creators are widely thought to be stronger.”).

    Sources indicate that political ad tech firms are noticing that influence. “When you can have trusted messengers really resonating with an audience, whether you’re trying to sell a product or convince someone to vote for a candidate, having that trusted messenger is really a powerful thing,” explained Mark Jablonowski, CEO of DSPolitical, an ad-tech firm that works with candidates mostly on the Democratic side of the aisle. “Having the social sphere of people responding to the news and clipping and sharing in a very organic and viral way is an notable thing.”.

    Jablonowski said Republicans have historically utilized the MAGA network of influencers much more effectively in the past. “This was one of the first years that Democrats really spent significant resources and time on focusing on this, and it was definitely a component of their success,” he said, although he argued that the critical problems of broken promises, war and inflation had the single largest effect on the voter swing —far more than any media strategy had.

    It has been revealed that there’s little doubt even more ad dollars will be poured into the next presidential election than we witnessed this year. And it will start sooner than ever, with 2027 possibly enjoying more of a windfall of primary spending than any off-year, said Jablonowski. He cited local down ballot races as contributing to that expected increase.

    It has been revealed that “When we’re looking to 2028, we’re going to see more of these advanced technologies being attainable by the down ballot races,” he mentioned. “You’re just going to see all of the local races really utilizing this best in class tech because it is available and consumable.”.

    Sources indicate that fullPAC’s Trawick agreed that 2028 will break all the records that have been set before in every election cycle, presidential or midterm. “The question is whether campaigns keep spending the same way,” he saod. “They shouldn’t. 2027 and 2028 call for a different approach, and it starts with the calendar. The campaigns that win will blueprint earlier: introduce the candidate, build relationships and test messages long before broadcast rates spike.”.

    As far as preferred media, Jablonowski expects to see not only more CTV/streaming and creator investment by candidates, but also digital audio/streaming. “The plumbing has finally been plumbed in, where you can address audiences at scale through streaming audio, whether it be podcast or or music,” he said.

    StackAdapt’s political team, in an email to Digiday, remarked its expects well-funded presidential candidates could start buying ads to build name recognition as early as Q2 or Q3 next year, depending on when they enter the race.

    It has been revealed that expect to see TV, particularly linear, used less and in different ways. “Money follows what can be measured. We can expect to see more spending on channels that reach a specific voter and show you whether it worked: texting, CTV and streaming and targeted digital,” mentioned Trawick. “Broadcast won’t disappear, but late-cycle saturation gets harder to justify. Three weeks of TV at peak rates, aimed at people who already voted early, is the first line item that should get a hard look. The bigger shift is the calendar, not the channel. Early voting turned election day into a season, and budgets have to be built for the whole season.”.

    There’s really only one set of numbers that was key last week: sales of Grand Theft Auto’s 6th installment. According to Sensor Tower (numbers that have not yet been confirmed by Rockstar Games) pre-orders and first-day sales exceeded 24.5 million copies, generating approximately $2.36 billion. It’s widely considered one of the biggest entertainment blockbusters in any medium ever. So, if your brand isn’t too worried about brand safety or adjacency to hardcore content, maybe GTA 7, whenever that comes out, is the place to be.

    “John was one of the rare ones that could negotiate an entire marketplace — including sports, and he knew everything about the sports marketplace — but didn’t have to just be a specialist … with John leaving the business, we are going to be missing one of the true intellectual hearts of the buying side.”.

    #158368. Hybrid won the in-housing debate, at least among the largest advertisers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Hybrid won the in-housing debate, at least among the largest advertisers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • In a recent development, reports of the media agency’s death remain greatly exaggerated.
    • Advertisers are carving up the media operation with more intent, keeping the work that sits closest to the brand and handing the sprawling specialist stuff back to their agencies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    In a recent development, reports of the media agency’s death remain greatly exaggerated. Its job description, however, is another story.

    Advertisers are carving up the media operation with more intent, keeping the work that sits closest to the brand and handing the sprawling specialist stuff back to their agencies.

    The shift has been playing out in fits and starts for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey shows how far its got. The media agency research firm polled 28 senior marketing, media, procurement and operations leaders at 21 global advertisers, who between them control more than $22 billion in media spend. A quarter of them buy or control media in-house. Of the rest, around a third are thinking about bringing spend in-house over the next 12 months.

    “It’s a bit like a football club,” said Jon Williams, founder and chief creative officer at Freedom Works, a collective of senior agency execs who help brands build in-house teams. “You build your own academy and you’re proud of it. You still buy a striker when you need goals. You just don’t keep a dozen agents on the payroll in case.”.

    It has been revealed that whether they’ve started in-housing or are still weighing it up, few advertisers want to take everything off their agency’s plate. Most would rather divide the work. Nearly 80% of respondents described their setup as hybrid, mixing internal teams with agency support. Fewer than 18% run media entirely in-house.

    Sources indicate that “The CMO isn’t always the one pushing,” said Scott Grenz, head of U.S. operations for COMvergence. “Much of the energy comes from internal media, procurement and data/analytics teams. They believe owning their data and getting full transparency are key to media effectiveness, and that often leads to bringing parts of the digital media scope in-house.

    “Agencies have become more transparent, and advertisers are looking at their media ecosystem as a whole, asking how best to use all their resources, internal and external, to hit their critical KPIs, said Grenz.

    Which is to say the motive for in-housing has moved from saving money to getting better at specific things. Mars is staffing internal teams to get ready for agentic shopping, while Gap has gone as far as setting up its own entertainment studio. Lego brought programmatic in-house partly so it could make better informed calls on which ad tech vendors to use. Its agency, and its vendors, can expect sharper questions as a result.

    “When I started out, the in-house studio was where ads went to get resized,” stated Williams. “The agency did the thinking and the studio did the cutdowns. Nobody would say that now.”.

    Getting here took the best part of a decade. For most of that time, in-housing was a cost and transparency play with advertisers chasing cheaper media and a clearer view of where the money went. The ANA’s 2016 report on agency rebates gave plenty of them reason to look. Somewhere along the way, the question moved on to what their own teams could do faster or better.

    In a recent development, in-house teams tend to go where the budgets are, which for most advertisers means digital. The largest group of respondents put 60% to 70% of total media spend into digital and plenty go higher, according to the report. Only a very small minority keep digital below 30%.

    Unsurprisingly, social media is where advertisers are most willing to take the wheel. More than 85% of the in house operators in the survey run social themselves. Search display and programmatic trail at roughly 57%. The logic is simple enough. Social rewards fast decisions and direct access to audience data, both of which come easier when the team sits inside the business.

    Recent findings suggest that the same can’t be said of retail media, CTV and influencer marketing. They remain mostly agency-run, with relatively few advertisers taking them on directly. All three are fragmented and specialized enough to keep agencies in demand. Take Retail media. Its sprawl of networks and measurement approaches is the sort of mess advertisers seem happy to pay someone else to untangle. Several respondents still named influencer, commerce and retail media as where they’re experimenting with newly introduced models or looking for outside guidance.

    According to recent reports, “Building an in-house media practice is hard. It carries real risk, takes significant resources and requires capabilities many advertisers don’t have yet,” mentioned Grenz.” Still, there are plenty of use cases across the industry, from big advertisers and small, and no single model has won out. Our data highlights that many advertisers who have in-housed still work with a media agency. That’s the real takeaway: it isn’t all or nothing. Advertisers are working out the right mix of internal and external expertise to make their media effective.”.

    It has been revealed that for all the talk of brands doing more on their own, agency rosters remain crowded. More than half (54) of the marketers COMvergence interviewed use more than one media agency and more than half bring in digital specialist agencies alongside their main one.

    Still, that crowding probably won’t last. More than 80% of the advertisers working with multiple agencies plan to simplify or consolidate. They want specialist expertise and fewer partners at the same time — a tension that should keep the pitch consultants busy for a while.

    “Some of it is procurement,” said Williams. “One in-house lead told us it took nine months to get a newly introduced supplier set up. Do that ten times and you’ll consolidate too. And AI is taking away a lot of the everyday work that used to keep four or five agencies busy.”.

    Half of the respondents use global hubs, offshore resources or both. Their comments pointed to India, Colombia, Brazil, Mexico and other regional centers, mostly handling digital operations, programmatic buying, social execution and support work.

    Recent findings suggest that advertisers see these setups as agency-run rather than as their own teams. That’s a handy calling card for holdcos selling scale. In fact, COMvergence expects hubs and offshore talent to become an even bigger differentiator for agencies as labor costs rise and more execution gets automated.

    “There’s no universal ceiling,” mentioned Grenz. “It comes down to how each advertiser weighs the risk and reward of in-housing against agency management. Agencies have made a strong case that they’re a critical partner, and they’ve shown they’re willing to work within whatever hybrid model a client wants.”.

    Industry observers note that asked what they’d like more of, respondents pointed squarely at agency operating models, which made up more than 40% of all feedback. They want to see how peers structure internal teams, split work between brand and agency, govern media investment and run in-house functions.

    Industry observers note that the usual caveats apply to a report like this. Twenty one advertisers is a small sample so a handful of companies can swing a percentage by a lot. COMvergence plans to run the survey every year and the second edition should say more about the direction of travel than this first snapshot can.

    Even so, the findings are a good encapsulation of how senior marketers at the largest advertisers see where things are headed.

    Breaking: Brands boost Black Friday CTV, retail and search spending

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • Brands are expected to spend 10-30% more on digital media activity over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, compared with 2025, according to five media buyers who spoke with Digiday.
    • Industry observers note that spending growth around Black Friday (Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Brands are expected to spend 10-30% more on digital media activity over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, compared with 2025, according to five media buyers who spoke with Digiday. Retail media, particularly Amazon, search, CTV and YouTube, are expected to soak up much of that increase.

    Industry observers note that spending growth around Black Friday (Nov. 27) and Cyber Monday (Nov. 30), the twin peaks of the holiday season for many retailers, hardly comes as a surprise. According to Triple Whale, 33,000 U.S. brands spent $607 million across the Black Friday/Cyber Monday period last year; this year, Bain Capital estimates U.S. companies to record $85 billion in sales over the five day period, accounting for 8.5% of total holiday spending for 2026.

    But there’s nuance to be considered, especially with retailers choosing to discount earlier in the year.

    “We expect higher spend across direct-response channels this year, though it varies by category and brand,” stated Brett Fischer, associate director of performance media at e-commerce-focused media agency Collective Measures.

    In a recent development, for one, product discounting and marketing activity kicked off earlier this year. According to commerce media company Fluent, 32% of shoppers had already begun holiday purchases prior to Black Friday.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, the number of products listed at a discount between Oct. 1-20 rose 56%, and increased 71% during the week preceding Prime Big Deal Days, according to data from e-commerce firm Wayvia. In 2025, the same discounting surge didn’t kick in until the middle of November.

    That’s driven budget increases, or forced some marketers to spread their ad dollars over a longer period of time. Nola Ladd, associate director of brand media at Collective Measures, said the agency’s clients had spread their ad dollars thinner over a longer period, with the aim of improving consumer consideration.

    “Mid-funnel investment is running roughly flat year over year,” said Ladd. “Instead of growing it in this period, we’ve spread it across more of the year so brands are building consideration well before peak season.”.

    In a recent development, U.S. retail sales are expected to rise 4.2% this year compared with 2025, according to Oxford Economics, while the National Retail Federation (NRF) estimated that 182.7 million Americans will shop during the five-day run of discounts and sales, a slight reduction from 2025’s 186.9 million.

    For some retailers, heavy discounting in the run-up to Black Friday is beginning to bite. Data from media agency PMG found that weekly sales rose 10% during October’s Prime Big Deal Days (staged by Amazon on Oct. 6-7), with grocery purchases increasing 37.7% in volume. But the average selling price in that category fell 13.1%, while electronics revenues were “flat.”.

    “Many of our clients in CPG and home delivery are watching sell-through closely,” remarked Scott Shamberg, president and CEO at media agency Mile Marker.

    “Many of our clients saw softness for the last few weeks but are still expecting to see demand and sales pick up,” said Michelle Merklin, vp of search innovation and growth, Tinuiti.

    According to recent reports, companies affected by tariff-related cost increases will have to choose between crucial profit margin or the need to match competitors’ discounts. “It’s crucial for brands to continue to stay competitive within this time frame,” said Carly Carson, head of integrated media at PMG.

    “Our clients’ spend this Black Friday and Cyber Monday is mixed — some are flat and some are up. There has been some softening in the market the last quarter, so some clients are being conservative,” stated Josy Amann, co-founder, Ars X Machina (AXM).

    Per PMG data, brands that discounted across a larger range of their portfolio enjoyed a lot more growth during October: on average, those with 75% of their product set on discount saw 16% overall revenue growth, while companies that discounted 25% or less of their products saw overall revenues fall 11%.

    Sales softness, and increased cost of sales hasn’t led to clients risking a retreat from Black Friday spending — the weekend window is too important a sales event for retailers. “We have definitely been making strong recommendations around maintaining a full-funnel strategy… BFCM is a great time to find upcoming consumers in a shopping mindset,” stated Amann.

    According to recent reports, but some advertisers were shifting dollars into channels considered to be safer bets. “Less brand, more performance channels,” Shamberg explained. Merklin also noted Tinuiti clients were, on the whole, choosing not to cut media budgets.

    Those safer bets include CTV and YouTube, as well as retail media options. According to Brock Berry, CEO of digital ad trafficking platform AdCellerant, the quantity of advertisers running CTV activity during November was 25% than the same period last year, despite CPMs running as much as 18% higher in some regions following high competition from political spenders during the midterm elections. Shamberg stated he expected to see “double-digit growth” in each of those channels among Mile Marker clients.

    Sources indicate that at the same time, product discovery behaviors are under question. A survey of 29,000 consumers commissioned by delivery organization DHL estimated that 90% of shoppers used generative AI chatbots or assistants to compare prices, while half said they used the tools to browse.

    As such, marketers are paying close attention to search, Merklin noted. She said Tinuiti clients were expected to spend 11 to 15% more with Google compared with last year, with total search spending up 11% versus 2025. Clients’ standalone display campaign spending had largely shifted into the tech giant’s Demand Gen and Performance Max campaigns, which rose 30% and both include display and video inventory.

    Sources indicate that PMG’s Carson mentioned clients were spending on social as well, with an eye to influencing product discovery, while also increasing CTV investments. “That’s an area where we expect investment to be up well into the double digits year-over-year,” she said.

    Recent findings suggest that “[It’s] something I don’t see slowing down in 2027,” addedCarson. “More advanced targeting capabilities here, including around placing ads during specific content contexts, are going to make it easier for brands to further invest.”.

    HUMAN Security’s latest investigation queries the effectiveness of CTV verification safeguards.

    According to recent reports, the shift has been playing for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey shows had far its got. T.

    With more than $12 billion spent this year, expectations are that number will only rise in 2028, with lots more spent as early as Q2 2027. Where will it be spent?

    Gap Inc. posted its earnings results for the third quarter of 2026 on Thursday, with double-digit growth from the Gap brand offsetting declines from Athleta and Banana Republic.

    “Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency and underlying health of the brand is giving us real confidence in the brand’s ability to continue its momentum,” noted Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson on Thursday’s earnings call. “Our customer file continues to grow, particularly as we attract newer Gen Z customers, but we’re doing it while we’re preserving the brand’s multi-generational appeal.”.

    In a recent development, gap’s net sales were up 11% to $1.1 billion, and Old Navy’s net sales rose 1% to $2.3 billion. Meanwhile, Athleta’s net sales fell 14% to $220 million, and Banana Republic declined 3% to $449 million. The manufacturer as a whole reported a 2% increase in net sales to $4 billion.

    Dickson cited additional releases from Gap’s collaborations with Hailey Bieber and Victoria Beckham as boosting sales in the period, along with the brand’s reentry into the beauty category. The company did not share specific figures from the revival of Gap’s classic ‘90s fragrances like Grass and Dream in July, but called the early response “encouraging.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the tech giant is doubling down on creating what it calls “fashiontainment,” Dickson shared. Following the appointment of Pam Kaufman as evp, chief entertainment officer in January, Gap Inc. has tapped boy band Just Your Type (JYT) for a multi-year partnership and debuted “The Agency,” a scripted microseries made for Banana Republic. Looking ahead, Dickson noted Gap will also co-produce a docuseries.

    “We see our fashiontainment platform as a recognized way of how customers aren’t just buying apparel today; they’re buying into brands that are telling compelling stories and driving cultural conversations,” remarked Dickson.

    Recent findings suggest that gap is far from the only brand to attempt to extend its cultural relevance through entertainment. Gap collaborator and founder of her namesake brand Victoria Beckham was the subject of a 2025 docuseries made with Netflix and Studio 99, her husband David Beckham’s production company. Maybelline launched a Christmas-themed “microdrama” in 2025, while reveals like “Nobody Wants This” have featured a growing level of product placement with the likes of Estée Lauder and La Bonne Brosse.

    Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

    Consulting giants Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

    With shareholders, an $895 billion compute bill and a costly free tier, Anthropic’s no-ads pledge may have a shelf life.

    • Poydenis spent more than 10 years building Influential, which he and his partners sold to Publicis in 2024 for $500 million, according to the company.
    • Sources indicate that poydenis is also bringing along Jesse Batres, most recently the executive vice president and head of national sales and partnerships at Influential, to BuzzFeed, where he will serve as its latest president of sales and partnerships.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The digital media publisher BuzzFeed has hired Chris Poydenis, the co-founder and longtime chief revenue officer of the influencer marketing organization Influential, as its latest chief revenue officer, the company revealed Monday.

    Poydenis spent more than 10 years building Influential, which he and his partners sold to Publicis in 2024 for $500 million, according to the company.

    Sources indicate that poydenis is also bringing along Jesse Batres, most recently the executive vice president and head of national sales and partnerships at Influential, to BuzzFeed, where he will serve as its latest president of sales and partnerships. Both executives start Monday.

    Recent findings suggest that “I had breakfast with [CEO Byron Allen], and it didn’t take more than 30 minutes for me to be completely aligned and bought in,” Poydenis noted. “BuzzFeed already has such beloved brands—with Tasty and HuffPost. There’s an incredible base to build from.”.

    The hires come at a precarious moment for BuzzFeed. Six months after Allen took a controlling stake in the company, the publisher has cut more than a third of its staff, and its stock has cratered, all while it tries to reinvent itself as a video-first, free-streaming platform.

    Whether that pivot works will depend largely on whether advertisers follow BuzzFeed into the living room, a job that will now fall to Poydenis and Batres.

    Under its new ownership, BuzzFeed aims to pair content from its existing brands with premium content from Allen Media Group and distribute it across a connected television app, the website, and the mobile app, according to Poydenis.

    The publisher also looks to expand into user-generated and creator content, according to The Fresh York Times.

    “If you look at what other streaming platforms are doing, they are all clamoring to figure out a way to infuse the creator economy into their product,” Poydenis mentioned. “With [Batres] and I coming over, we’re in lockstep with [Allen] to make that a reality.”.

    FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context.

    Industry observers note that the goal is to recruit more creators and build a platform where they can upload their libraries and monetize them with brands. In doing so, the creators would be adding to BuzzFeed’s 75 million monthly active people and 2 billion monthly content views, according to Poydenis.

    Still, the odds facing the firm are long.

    Sources indicate that allen took over as chairman and CEO in May, after his holding firm, Allen Family Digital, agreed to pay $120 million for a 52% stake: $20 million at closing and the remaining $100 million over five years. In tandem with the deal, cofounder Jonah Peretti stepped down as CEO to become its new president of AI.

    Before the deal, BuzzFeed had warned investors that it was at risk of not continuing as a business, citing $58.4 million in debt and millions in annual losses, according to The New York Times.

    Sources indicate that in July, the company laid off about 180 employees across BuzzFeed, HuffPost, and Tasty, roughly 35% of its workforce, according to an SEC filing. Earlier this month, its stock fell 38% in a single morning after a disappointing third-quarter earnings report, sinking to $0.57 per share, according to Futurism.

    For Poydenis, the turnaround is part of the appeal.

    Recent findings suggest that “At my heart, I’m a competitor, and I’m a builder,” Poydenis noted. “After the acquisition with Publicis, I feel like for me the job was done. [Allen] is offering me an opportunity to go in somewhere with a phenomenal foundation and to build once again.”.

    Mark Stenberg is ADWEEK's senior media reporter.

    #158354. Breaking: The Rundown: BADBOX 3.0, the CTV ad fraud scheme generating 40 billion bid requests a day

    Breaking: The Rundown: BADBOX 3.0, the CTV ad fraud scheme generating 40 billion bid requests a day

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.
    • Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.

    Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.

    Industry observers note that the Nov. 18 disclosure raises fresh questions about the effectiveness of CTV ad fraud detection — and how much fraudulent inventory slips through existing safeguards, notable gaps for the industry to collectively plug as marketers increasingly spend ad dollars on such channels.

    According to HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence team, the situation involved a network of compromised, low-cost Android-based streaming devices running malware designed to generate fraudulent video advertising activity without their owners’ knowledge.

    The operation was more than three times larger, by peak daily bid-request volume, than VASTFLUX, previously the largest publicly disclosed scheme measured on that basis.

    Researchers linked elements of the malware distribution infrastructure to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, identifying connections involving device software, code repositories and command-and-control servers.

    HUMAN also uncovered links to earlier BADBOX operations, including BADBOX 2.0, which was exposed in 2025 and involved more than 10 million compromised devices across 222 countries and territories.

    The latest discovery illustrates how fraud operations can reconstitute themselves following earlier disruptions, adapting their infrastructure and techniques to evade detection.

    The malware then installed advertising software on infected devices, allowing video commercials to play in hidden windows while customers continued watching television or navigating their streaming interfaces.

    The resulting advertising requests impersonated legitimate CTV applications, making the inventory appear authentic to downstream buyers.

    Some fraudulent requests also originated from residential proxy networks, helping disguise their source as ordinary household internet traffic.

    HUMAN identified 11 proxy networks in which compromised devices could be enrolled without their owners’ consent, effectively turning consumer internet connections into infrastructure available for third-party use. Separately, researchers uncovered spoofed server-side ad insertion traffic, in which fraudulent requests purported to represent advertisements inserted into streaming sessions that did not actually exist.

    The scale of the operation is considerable, although its financial impact remains unclear.

    Recent findings suggest that crucially, the 40 billion figure represents bid requests, not completed advertising transactions or billable impressions. Consequently, it cannot be used to calculate advertiser losses without establishing how much fraudulent inventory was purchased.

    Industry observers note that hence, the question remains: what proportion of the 40 billion daily bid requests became paid impressions? And how much money was spent on invalid inventory?

    However, due to the intricacies of online ad auctions – where CPMs can vary significantly – HUMAN was unable to provide an exact dollar amount when asked about the financial impact of the operation.

    Nonetheless, sources approached by Digiday estimated that BADBOX 3.0 could potentially have cost advertisers millions of dollars per day at its height.

    Shailin Dhar, partner at Futureproof TMT, cautioned against equating the operation’s 40 billion daily bid requests with actual advertiser losses, noting that CTV supply audited by his firm since 2024 has averaged a fill rate of approximately 2%. He further counseled that fraudulent inventory originating from low-end applications and devices could perform considerably worse.

    At this juncture, it’s worth considering that enormous volumes of fraudulent auction traffic do not necessarily translate into equivalent volumes of wasted advertising expenditure. At an illustrative fill rate of 0.5% and realized revenue of $3 per thousand impressions, 40 billion daily requests would generate approximately $600,000 in revenue. However, Dhar stressed that such calculations should not be mistaken for evidence of the operation’s actual earnings.

    Nevertheless, the operation’s ability to masquerade as legitimate streaming inventory highlights potential weaknesses in how CTV advertising transactions are authenticated.

    Recent findings suggest that CTV has become an increasingly notable channel for advertisers seeking to reach audiences migrating from traditional television. However, its programmatic infrastructure also presents opportunities for fraudsters to exploit fragmented supply paths and inconsistent verification practices.

    BADBOX 3.0 demonstrates how apparently legitimate app identifiers, residential IP addresses and video ad requests can be combined to manufacture the appearance of genuine viewing activity. The question is whether existing safeguards can consistently identify such behavior before advertisers are charged.

    Futureproof’s Dhar questioned the effectiveness of existing verification safeguards, arguing that private marketplaces and curated deals remain vulnerable because of limited device, content, and connection signals, alongside excessive confidence in identity matching.

    “My personal estimate is roughly a 90% chance that at least one comparable operation is running without public identification,” he told Digiday, while acknowledging that its scale and financial impact remain unknown.

    Per Dhar’s assessment, effective CTV verification requires persistent checks throughout the advertising supply chain, rather than relying exclusively on pre-bid or post-bid detection.

    For now, HUMAN says customers using its Ad Fraud Defense service are protected against the operation’s associated attacks, while its researchers continue monitoring the perpetrators for further adaptations.

    The findings come roughly a month after a separate investigation by ad security firm Confiant and researchers at Citizen Lab exposed how online advertising infrastructure was used to distribute spyware, highlighting another vulnerability in the digital advertising ecosystem.

    That investigation, detailed in research published by Citizen Lab, found that Israeli company Discover-Tech exploited targeted advertising mechanisms to deliver zero-click spyware, including attacks against devices at Al Jazeera.

    While the two operations differed in their objectives — one targeting advertising budgets, the other facilitating surveillance — both illustrate how infrastructure designed to connect advertisers with audiences can be repurposed for malicious activity.

    The broader concern is that BADBOX 3.0 is another iteration of an established threat rather than an isolated incident — and that dismantling one operation does not necessarily eliminate the infrastructure or incentives behind the next.

    Advertisers continue to increase investments on the retail weekend but AI, tariffs and discounting pressure present banana skins.

    Industry observers note that the shift has been playing for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey demonstrates had far its got. T.

    With more than $12 billion spent this year, expectations are that number will only rise in 2028, with lots more spent as early as Q2 2027. Where will it be spent?

    D+ Research: Brand’s holiday marketing tactics shift in 2026

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders.
    • In a recent development, this is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →.

    In a recent development, this is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies. The report is based on a survey of 90 brand and retailer professionals, as well as individual interviews with marketing executives.

    Digiday’s survey found that brands and retailers plan to adjust the marketing tactics they’ll use during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to those they used in 2025.

    The biggest changes are that CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026, with year-over-year increases of 22 percentage points and 20 percentage points, respectively.

    Sources indicate that forty-five percent of survey respondents noted they proposal to use CTV/streaming ads this holiday season, in comparison to 23% of respondents who said the same in 2025. The 2026 uptick followed a 14 percentage point dip in usage from 2024 to 2025.Meanwhile, marketers’ usage of TV ads remained relatively stable between 2024 and 2025, dropping by only 4 percentage points between 2024 and 2025, but grew by a whopping 20 percentage points in 2026. Thirty-three percent of brands and retailers said they plan to use TV ads this holiday season in comparison to 13% of marketers who said the same in 2025.

    “Streaming is a really valid channel to invest in during holiday because consumption of that media spikes,” said Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement tech giant Ritual. “But participating in streaming is actually a decision for the whole year. Starting to engage just for holiday would be a risky move, especially for a smaller brand.”.

    “If you have the data to back it up over the course of the year showing this is a channel that’s proven and the ROI metrics associated, it can make a lot of sense to spike it during holiday,” she added.

    Industry observers note that ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, said that both streaming and TV ads can be effective for targeting specific demographic groups during the holidays. “Streaming and television is an effective audience conversion mechanism, especially with women over 30 years old,” Bloom said. “We’ve done a lot of work on daytime TV and on QVC. We see significantly bigger segments in the holiday time period from November through mid-December, and we always put attention on those times.”.

    It has been revealed that last year, brands’ and retailers’ most-used holiday marketing tactic was brand experiences, but that strategy fell to second place in 2026 behind streaming/CTV ads. Forty-one percent of marketers noted they expect to use brand experiences as a marketing strategy during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to 50% of marketers who said the same in 2025 — a drop of 9 percentage points.

    Sources indicate that brands and retailers are also divesting from using gift guides and influencer hauls/unboxing videos this holiday season. Marketers’ usage of gift guides decreased by 19 percentage points in 2026 vs. 2025, while their use of influencer hauls/unboxing videos fell by 14 percentage points this year in comparison to last year.

    Although gift guides and brand experiences decreased in marketer usage for the 2026 holidays, they remain brands’ and retailers’ top performing holiday marketing tactics over time. Thirty-one percent of marketers said gift guides have historically performed the best for their company during the holiday season, while 28% of marketers said the same of brand experiences, putting them in the No. 1 and No. 2 ranking spots, respectively.

    Although some marketers are shifting away from using gift guides for the upcoming holiday season, Ritual’s Brodie said gift guides are likely to gain importance in the AI-driven search era because AI-powered search tools often rely on best of lists and curated recommendations to answer consumer queries.

    “Gift guides are very interesting in the world of AEO and thinking about LLM optimization,” Brodie said. “Overall, best of lists and gift guides are a close sister to [AI search results]. Gift guides can play an important role in holiday and especially bridging LLM research and AI overviews. So, I’m bullish about gift guides.”.

    Although brands and retailers are leaning into CTV/streaming ads for the 2026 holidays, those marketing tactics tied in the No. 4 spot for the best-performing holiday marketing tactic over time, while pop-up shops ranked No. 3. Influencer hauls/unboxing videos was the only marketing strategy that fell in both best historic performance and marketers’ intended use during the 2026 holiday season.

    Industry observers note that A-Frame Brands’ Bloom stated brands and retailers should also consider investing in catalogs for the 2026 holiday. “Catalogs have always been very successful, and they’re heavily conversion-focused,” Bloom explained. “When they’re discount-driven and when people’s attention is on buying, you can do offers that you can only get via physical paper, and it does drive people into stores.”.

    #158343. Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (821 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • In a recent development, agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story.
    • Clients do not hire agencies to be fast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Amol Waishampayan, co-founder, fullthrottle.ai.

    In a recent development, agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story. Faster work, leaner teams, lower fees. Clients took the meeting, nodded along and then waited for the invoice to shrink. It didn’t. AI strategies now sound interchangeable to clients, who say the savings never indicated up in their fees.

    That is not an AI problem. It is a positioning problem. Efficiency was the wrong promise. Clients do not hire agencies to be fast. They hire them to grow the business. AI’s real opportunity for agencies is not doing the same work cheaper. It is doing work that actually moves revenue, and proving it.

    Agencies are getting operational value from AI. According to the Digiday Media Agency Report 2026, 70% of agencies say AI has cut costs by making tasks more efficient, while 31% say it cost more to implement than expected. But efficiency is a one-time gain.

    Once every agency has it, nobody gets paid for it. As one Gartner analyst told Digiday, the honeymoon between agencies and AI is “essentially over.” The agencies that build their AI story on productivity are competing on margin. The ones that build it on performance are competing on value, and value is what clients renew.

    Industry observers note that most media looks are still organized by channel. Search budget here, social budget there, streaming over in a separate deck. AI makes that structure obsolete, because it can proposal around the customer instead.

    Take a regional home services company running paid search and social. Those campaigns are producing something more valuable than clicks: a live stream of households actively researching its services. AI can turn those signals into a defined first-party audience, figure out where else those households spend their time, and extend the blueprint into streaming TV, digital video and audio to reach them there. One audience, coordinated across channels, built from the client’s own demand rather than a platform’s inventory.

    Industry observers note that that is a different kind of planning. The question stops being “what should we spend on CTV” and becomes “who are we trying to reach, and where are they?”.

    The next step is letting AI act on that intelligence. Agentic systems can take audience and performance signals and adjust targeting, channel mix and spend as conditions change, instead of waiting for the monthly optimization meeting. Static intends with quarterly reviews are a relic of how long it used to take humans to read the data.

    But here is where agencies should be careful. The advantage is not how much of the buying you automate. Anyone can automate. The advantage is whether the agent is optimizing toward something that matters. An agent chasing cheaper CPMs will find them, and the client will not care. An agent optimizing toward the client’s actual business outcomes, with the agency keeping full transparency and control, is a different product entirely.

    According to recent reports, this is the part most of the industry still avoids. Clicks and impressions are easy to report and nearly impossible to defend in a budget conversation. The only metrics a CFO cares about are sales, customers and revenue.

    AI makes closing that gap practical. Bring together the advertiser’s first-party customer data, its transaction history and campaign exposure, and one can see which households were reached, which ones became customers and which channels and audiences did the work. Done with privacy-first, household-level methods rather than individual tracking, this is not surveillance. It is the client’s own data finally answering the client’s own question.

    Recent findings suggest that once that loop exists, everything upstream improves. Planning gets smarter because it is fed by real conversions. Agentic buying gets better because it is optimizing toward revenue instead of proxies. And the agency walks into every renewal with proof rather than a deck.

    Sources indicate that agencies are already monetizing AI. Digiday’s report found that 59% are launching fresh AI-powered products, 34% are selling strategic roadmaps or audits and 31% are charging additional fees for AI-powered services. But if the product is “we have AI,” the pricing power will not last. Every competitor has AI. Within a year, every client will have it too.

    The agencies that win the next cycle will not be the ones with the most AI. They will be the ones who can show a client exactly what it delivered, in the client’s own numbers. Efficiency gets agencies a thank-you. Outcomes get agencies the next three years of the account.Partner insights from fullthrottle.ai.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (782 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    The next test for agentic media

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.
    • Sources indicate that advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.

    Sources indicate that advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work. These teams have their own agents, their own data and their own rules for what an agent may and may not do. At the same time, most of the specialized intelligence they depend on still sits inside separate vendor platforms.

    According to recent reports, as a result, vendor intelligence shapes a recommendation while remaining disconnected from the system acting on the recommendation. When planners carry conclusions between tools, the evidence and conditions behind those recommendations often fall away.

    It has been revealed that that’s the problem agentic media has to solve next. Can the intelligence behind the agent go where the work happens?

    Recent findings suggest that models and agent frameworks are widely available. Two vendors can build on the same foundation and ship agents that look identical in a demo. What separates them is what the agent knows, and whether the advertiser can put that knowledge to work. In media buying, that knowledge is specific.

    In a recent development, A broad content classification offers only a starting point for a media decision. Suitability depends on the particular advertiser and market, and those judgments can change rapidly when breaking news alters the significance of a placement. A general-purpose model can’t reconstruct that brand-specific knowledge or historical context from a prompt alone. Classification depth and performance history can.

    Industry observers note that for Channel Factory, that means IAB 3.0 classification across more than 15 million YouTube channels, and more than 10 years and $4 billion of campaign performance data. To be clear, this isn’t an argument for keeping that intelligence locked inside a platform; it’s the opposite. Intelligence that only works inside its owner’s interface is as limited as a capable agent no one can reach.

    So the test is portability. Can an advertiser’s own agent call on a provider’s intelligence directly, from inside the planning and buying environment it already uses? That’s how Channel Factory is building, with contextual and suitability intelligence made available through APIs and MCP servers, and delivered through modular agents that run inside an advertiser’s environment or alongside it.

    With this architecture, market-specific suitability analysis becomes part of an advertiser’s own planning process. An agent can evaluate inventory against the provider’s classifications and historical performance data, applying the relevant standards for each market. Those findings can directly inform the proposal, with the advertiser’s existing rules governing what the agent can recommend or change.

    Sources indicate that portable intelligence doesn’t mean identical agents. Two advertisers can draw on the same underlying intelligence and make different decisions. For instance, one avoids content when signals are unclear while another favors reaching inside defined boundaries. Both are valid because the thresholds, priorities and approval rules are the advertisers’.

    According to recent reports, an agent’s knowledge source shouldn’t determine the scope of its authority. The brand decides what acceptable judgment looks like. The provider keeps the classification, history and models current.

    Learning needs the same discipline. Feedback and outcomes should refine recommendations, but advertisers should decide what shapes future decisions and which policies stay fixed. On its own, a successful campaign shouldn’t rewrite a brand’s suitability standards.

    Intelligence that moves into someone else’s systems has to carry its accountability along. As agents shift from recommending to acting, teams need to see what changed, why and whether it stayed within approved limits.

    The principle is simple: Agents do the reasoning, and the engine owns the state, so every action is authorized, logged and traceable to the signals behind it. People define the strategy. Autonomy is earned in stages: alerts first, then recommendations, then bounded actions. An agent might make a small budget adjustment under set conditions while sending a larger change for human approval. How much authority to delegate is the advertiser’s call, and the system should make that call easy to enforce and easy to review.

    Recent findings suggest that as agentic capabilities spread, feature lists will converge. Advertisers should look underneath the interface and put three questions to any provider:.

    The providers who can answer those clearly will matter more as brands take greater control of how they buy media. The rest will be unrealized demos.

    Partner insights from Channel Factory.

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.     Curious about the kind of challenges you'll work on at Camunda? Watch this quick 30-minute talk from our engineers to learn more about the upcoming Camunda Exporter and how we’re solving complex problems at scale.

    According to recent reports, we are looking for a Product Builder to join the IDP & RPA pod. You will take real problems from customers, decide what is worth solving, and build and ship the solution yourself, using AI tools to get from idea to production swiftly without lowering the bar.

    Recent findings suggest that product Building is how Camunda's Experience organization builds the applications people use on top of Camunda 8, such as Hub, Operate, and ProcessOS. Small pods of builders own a product area from customer problem to shipped change, with no hand-offs between product management, design, and engineering. We are setting this model up now, so you will help shape how it works.

    The IDP & RPA pod builds how Camunda processes work with documents and legacy applications. With intelligent document processing (IDP), customers create extraction and classification templates in Camunda Hub and publish them so a process can use AI to turn invoices and other documents into structured data. With robotic process automation (RPA), customers integrate legacy applications that have no APIs, using Robot Framework scripts on a standalone RPA worker. The hard problems come with putting LLMs into customer processes: extraction quality, model and prompt choices, testing and trust, and working for AI agents as well as for people.

    Help shape product direction for IDP & RPA by combining customer input, usage data, and field feedback into clear priorities.

    Partner with the other builders and product strategy to turn problems into shipped features, using short written proposals and prototypes to align early.

    Make judgment calls with incomplete information within your scope and own the outcome.

    Communicate trade-offs and decisions clearly to stakeholders who don't live in the details the way you do.

    Use AI tools across the whole loop, from specs to prototypes to production-ready code, and hold a high bar for what you ship by reviewing and improving the output rather than accepting it.

    Build, test, and ship improvements to the IDP & RPA experience, reading errors and tracing issues far enough to give your pod useful context.

    Talk to customers and to support and customer success colleagues about how IDP is used and where it breaks, and turn what you learn into decisions about what to build next.

    Pick up customer incidents and trace them across Hub, the connectors, and the deployed process of the customer.

    Track what you ship against real outcomes and adjust when the data tells you to.

We are looking forward to your application!

    In a recent development, we're looking for a Head of Ecosystem to lead the teams that make Supabase the backend for the platforms and tools developers already use. That covers AI app builders and coding agents, integrations with the developer tools teams rely on, and the Supabase Marketplace. You'll build this org from the ground up and shape how Supabase extends beyond its own platform.

    You'll also drive hiring, onboarding, and career development while maintaining high engineering standards.

    Build and lead a new engineering org across platform partners, integrations, and Marketplace, hiring EMs and engineers as it grows.

    Own the technical relationship with the platforms building on Supabase, from integration health to escalations.

    Set and maintain clear roadmaps that balance partner needs with platform priorities.

    Partner with Product, Partnerships, and Sales to define and execute our ecosystem strategy.

    Ship a unified, self-serve surface for integrations and Marketplace.

    Maintain high engineering standards: roadmap hygiene, issue tracking, on-call, incident response, and responsiveness to partners.

    Proven experience leading multiple engineering teams, including managing other managers.

    Experience building and running platform, API, or integration surfaces that third parties depend on in production.

    Technical credibility with partner engineering teams, and the judgment to say no.

    Experience building teams or an org from a small base, including hiring and developing engineering managers.

    Strong organizational and execution skills: setting roadmaps, driving accountability, and keeping teams moving under uncertainty.

    Experience managing remote, globally distributed teams.

    Excellent cross-functional communication skills, especially with Product and commercial teams.

    Collaborative, low-ego, and adaptable.

    Have experience with OAuth, platform APIs, or app marketplaces.

    Have worked on a developer platform's partner or app ecosystem.

    Have worked with AI app builders or coding agents.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Sources indicate that once a year, the entire company gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Industry observers note that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    According to recent reports, hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

    In a recent development, we are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

    In a recent development, you will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling new features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

    It has been revealed that camunda is an AI-first company, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

    This is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

    Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

    Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for newly introduced features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

    Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce complications, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

    It has been revealed that build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

    Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

    On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

    Experience at a SaaS or software product tech giant, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

    Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

    Industry observers note that threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

    It has been revealed that you read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

    You build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

    Clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

    Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

    Sources indicate that willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

    Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

    Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

    Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

    Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    Sources indicate that we offer competitive, fair, and transparent compensation. Salary ranges are location-based, with Standard and Major markets (global tech hubs) reflecting local competition.

    The Annual Total Target Cash (base salary + 100% variable target, where applicable) shown below spans from the minimum in a Standard market to the maximum in a Major market. Final offers depend on skills, experience, and location, and we typically hire in the first half of the range to allow room for growth:.

    United States: $119,900.00 to $193,200.00.

    United Kingdom: £75,300.00 to £123,800.00.

    Singapore: S$148,900.00 to S$223,300.00.

    If you’re based elsewhere, you’ll be hired via Remote.com (our global employer partner), and your Talent Acquisition Partner will provide a personalized Total Rewards Calculator after your first interview.

    Equity: We also offer equity (where applicable) through our Virtual Stock Option Plan (VSOP).

    According to recent reports, we invest in your wellbeing, growth, and ability to connect, along with perks that support you no matter where you’re based. Our benefits are globally designed and locally delivered where applicable.

    Remote & Flexible: Work from anywhere with the setup that suits you, home office budget, co-working space support, and flexible time off to recharge when you need it.

    In Person Connection: We invest in meaningful face time through our Annual Kickoff (Vienna in 2025, Madrid in 2026!), team offsites, and Camundi Connection Budgets, including contributing to meetups while travelling,, and local gatherings with fellow Camundi.

    Health & Wellbeing: Access locally tailored healthcare, Modern Health for global mental wellbeing, and our Live Well Lifestyle Spending Account (LSA), a flexible, global benefit that puts you in control of your whole life, not just work, from: staying active, to caring for family, exploring personal passions, meaningful experiences, and investing in your financial wellbeing. The Live Well program debuts in 2026 and scales to €1,000 annually from 2027.

    Financial Security: Retirement and pension plans (often with company contributions), plus life and disability insurance where relevant.

    Professional Growth: Up to $/€/£1,000 per year for self-driven learning: courses, certifications, books, you decide!

We are looking forward to your application!
